readerTitle: Why some shoppers pay double for the same pill
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Bronnenberg 외 2015, 진통제 구매와 브랜드 프리미엄) + 가상 사례 (지역 슈퍼마켓 체인, 제조회사 사내 분석팀) · 가격은 설명용
insight: 브랜드가 해자인지는 얼마나 알려졌는지가 아니라, 고객이 비교하지 않고 고르거나 더 비싸도 사는지로 판단한다. 이 신뢰는 시간이 쌓아야 생기므로 경쟁자가 돈으로 빨리 살 수 없다.
misconception: 이름이 널리 알려지거나 광고비를 많이 쓰면 브랜드 해자가 생긴다.

sources.text: Bronnenberg, B. J., Dubé, J.-P., Gentzkow, M., & Shapiro, J. M. (2015). Do Pharmacists Buy Bayer? Informed Shoppers and the Brand Premium. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(4).
카드 1의 가격($4, $9)과 카드 2·8의 사업 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bronnenberg 외(2015)의 핵심 결과(약사·의사 등 제품을 잘 아는 소비자는 일반 소비자보다 두통약을 매장 자체 브랜드로 살 가능성이 훨씬 높다)를 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 비율을 쓰지 않고 'much more likely'로만 적었습니다.
논문 DOI(10.1093/qje/qjv024로 기억됨)를 확인한 뒤 sources의 url에 넣으세요.
카드 5 softwareNote의 'Nobody gets fired for choosing the big name'은 IBM에 관해 전해지는 업계 격언을 일반화한 표현입니다. 특정 인물의 인용으로 쓰지 않았습니다.
카드 1의 가격 $4와 $9는 설명용 가상 수치이며 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: Why some shoppers pay double for the same pill
body: Two boxes of headache pills sit side by side. Same active ingredient, same dose. The store brand costs $4. The famous brand costs $9.
Plenty of shoppers reach for the $9 box. They aren't foolish. They're paying for something real. The interesting question is who *doesn't* pay it.

image.label: Two headache pill boxes on a shelf, one plain, one famous
image.brief: 약국 선반 위 두통약 상자 두 개. 왼쪽은 단순한 흰색 자체 브랜드 상자에 "$4", 오른쪽은 화려한 상자에 "$9". 손 하나가 오른쪽 상자로 향하는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고·상표는 절대 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is this brand really powerful?
body: You run a regional chain of grocery stores. A national snack brand wants a bigger share of your shelf and says its name is "powerful." Your own store-brand version tastes almost the same and costs less.
Which sign would best prove the national brand has real power?

options.text: Nearly everyone in town recognizes its logo
options.feedback: Recognition helps, but people can know a name and still buy the cheaper box. Knowing isn't the same as paying.

options.text: Shoppers keep buying it at a higher price, even with your near-identical version right beside it
options.feedback: This is behavior, not opinion. If customers pay more when a cheaper copy is in reach, the name is doing real work.

options.text: It spends more on advertising than any rival
options.feedback: Spending shows effort, not results. Big budgets can buy attention for a while without earning lasting preference.

cards.title: The experts buy the cheap box.
body: Economists Bart Bronnenberg, Jean-Pierre Dubé, Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro studied millions of headache pill purchases in the US.
People who know the product best, such as pharmacists and doctors, were **much more likely** to buy the store brand than other shoppers. They know the pills are the same.
Everyone else faces uncertainty. Is the cheap one really as good? The famous name removes that worry. Shoppers pay extra for *trust*, not chemistry.

cards.title: Brand as a moat
body: A **brand moat** exists when trust or meaning tied to a name lets you charge more, or get chosen without being compared, in a way rivals can't copy quickly.
The test is behavior. Do customers pay a premium? Do they pick you first without shopping around? If not, you have a well-known name, not a moat.

image.label: A castle labeled 'trusted name' with a moat around it
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 성("Trusted name") 주변 해자에 "Years of kept promises"라고 적힌 물결. 해자 밖에서 경쟁자가 "Ad budget" 사다리를 들고 있지만 건너지 못함. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: You can buy attention. You can't buy history.
body: A rival with a bigger budget can make people know its name in months. Trust takes longer. It builds from:
list: **Consistency:** the product is the same every time
**Repeated experience:** each good purchase adds to the last
**Time:** years of promises kept with no big failures
cards.callout: That slow build is the moat. A rival can't skip the years.
cards.softwareNote: In software, brand matters most when buyers can't judge quality upfront and failure is costly, like payroll or security tools. The old saying "nobody gets fired for choosing the big name" is a brand moat at work.

cards.title: Brands matter most when buyers are unsure.
body: Brand moats are strongest when quality is hard to judge before buying, when a mistake is costly, or when the product says something about the buyer, like a gift or a watch.

They are weakest when comparing is easy. The pharmacist shows this: once you can judge quality yourself, the name stops being worth extra. Simple, repeat purchases with clear specs rarely support a big brand premium.

image.label: Scale from 'easy to compare' to 'hard to judge'
image.brief: 가로 스펙트럼 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Easy to compare"(설탕 봉지, 건전지), 오른쪽 "Hard to judge, costly to get wrong"(유아용 카시트, 수술, 선물용 시계). 오른쪽으로 갈수록 방패 아이콘이 커짐. 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: A brand is a promise, and promises can break.
body: Trust built over years can drop quickly after one visible failure, like a safety scare or a quiet cut in quality that customers notice.
A brand also limits you. Cutting corners to save money spends the very trust that lets you charge more. And as reviews and comparisons make quality easier to judge, the premium for trust can shrink.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead the analytics team at a manufacturer. Managers can hire outside consultants or use self-serve dashboard tools, but most come to you first. Your reputation: your numbers are never wrong.
Leadership asks you to halve turnaround time by dropping your double-check step. What do you do?

options.text: Drop the double-check everywhere to hit the target
options.feedback: You gain speed but spend the trust that makes managers skip the alternatives. One wrong number in a board report, and they start comparing.

options.text: Keep checks on high-stakes reports, and offer a faster tier clearly labeled as a draft
options.feedback: You protect the promise where it matters most and still get faster. The trade-off: more work explaining which tier is which.

options.text: Refuse any change, since your reputation will carry you
options.feedback: This guards the promise, but a brand isn't permanent. If you become too slow, the reason to choose you without comparing weakens.

cards.title: A brand is a moat only when it changes what customers do.
body: Fame isn't the test. Paying more, or choosing you without comparing, is. And it's built by keeping one promise for years.
**Try it today:** ask three recent customers why they chose you over the cheapest option. Answers about trust mean you have a brand. Answers about price or location mean you don't yet.
